description.text:
I believe the enduring value of crypto is not speculation, but better financial infrastructure. At its best, this technology gives people true sovereignty over their money, stronger property rights, greater freedom of movement, and a more open global economy.

Coinbase exists to accelerate that future. We build technology at the intersection of traditional and decentralized finance, making the path between them more seamless, reliable, and practical.

My work focuses on that interoperability layer: reducing the friction between old and new financial systems, and helping turn onchain capabilities from a separate ecosystem into infrastructure that can work at real-world scale.

That is what makes this space worth building in: not the noise, but the part that can actually matter.

I joined the React Native team at a pivotal moment. The framework already offered an unmatched developer experience, but it still had to prove itself in production: it was often flaky, struggled to integrate cleanly with other UI frameworks, and had clear performance limitations.

My focus was on closing that gap and making the promise real at scale. I initiated and drove the push for what became known as the React Native rearchitecture. Early on, I argued that the platform needed a new foundation, not another round of fixes layered over structural limitations. That effort became a deep technical reset that moved React Native forward by a full generation — think jumping from IE6 to Chrome 1. For six years in a row, I was also the project’s top contributor.

Over the next four years, React Native became the leading cross-platform UI framework, with a vibrant ecosystem of libraries, enormous adoption across the industry, and one of the largest open-source communities in the world. Our repository became the second most popular on GitHub by number of contributors. The architectural ideas behind that work also echoed far beyond React Native, influencing a broader wave of industry efforts such as Compose, Flutter, SwiftUI, and others.

I helped drive that transformation by improving the framework’s reliability, performance, and interoperability, while also strengthening the community around it.

At AnchorFree, I worked on technology with direct real-world impact. We were building consumer VPN products that protected private communication and preserved access to the open internet in places where censorship and network restrictions were part of daily life.

At the time, we were the largest consumer-focused VPN service in the world. Millions of people relied on our products to bypass restrictions, access information, and communicate more freely under oppressive internet controls.

My work focused on two areas that mattered most: product experience and unblockability. We improved the UI and ease of use so the product could grow, and we pushed hard on making the service harder for local network controls to detect and shut down. Both were essential: reach depended on usability, and impact depended on resilience.

It was some of the most meaningful product work of my career: software at massive scale, built to solve a real problem for real people.

Mobile messaging was becoming one of the defining product categories in consumer tech, and at ICQ I was part of a small team building directly in the middle of that shift. We were seven iOS engineers building a product that competed directly with much larger players like WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Telegram.

Despite our size, we operated at serious scale. ICQ served tens of millions of users and stayed especially strong in several local markets and online communities. We shipped fast, pushed product quality hard, and introduced many features before they became standard across the industry, including voice and video calls, stickers, GIFs, forwarding, group chats, and AR face filters.

My focus was on building fast, polished, highly interactive user experiences. We paid close attention to UI detail and performance, especially on weaker devices, where even a 300 ms stall on the main thread was serious enough to treat as a critical issue.

The result was a product that combined real scale, early innovation, and unusually strong UX execution in one of the most competitive spaces in mobile.

I started my career at Yandex, one of the few internet companies to seriously compete with Google in a major market. It was an unusually ambitious place to grow as an engineer: we moved fast, built aggressively, and often invented products before the path to execution was fully clear.

I worked on some of the company’s largest consumer and user-generated-content products, including photo hosting, social networking, messaging, and browser extensions. My focus was on interactive UI and frontend platform work — shipping features like tag-your-friends flows, type-ahead inputs, and core JavaScript building blocks at a time when those experiences still felt new.

Later, I helped build one of the earliest deeply customized Chromium-based browsers. That work became Yandex Browser, which went on to become Russia’s most widely used browser and a major driver of the company’s broader product ecosystem. My team delivered much of the browser’s user-facing UI and introduced features that were well ahead of standard browser UX at the time, including reader mode, adaptive bookmarks, built-in translation, privacy tools, and tighter integration with search and contextual data.

Yandex was where I learned how to build ambitious consumer software at scale — products with strong UX, real technical depth, and lasting market impact.

Developed UI of ICQ and MyChat for iPhone and iPad.

ICQ offers a range of services including text, voice and video calls, conference calls, file sharing, free SMS, online games, notifications of new messages and more.
ICQ is used monthly by 18 million people around the world.

Key role in development of core browser UI components.
(Yandex.Browser is a simple and easy-to-use internet browser.)
